questions.q: Which built-in utility type is the same as { [C in "NGN" | "USD"]: number }?
questions.explain: Record<K, V> is defined as { [P in K]: V }: one required property of type V per key.

questions.q: interface Row { readonly id: string; note?: string }. Which mapped type keeps id readonly and note optional?
questions.explain: A mapped type over keyof T is homomorphic and copies each property's modifiers. Looping over some other union of the same keys does not.
options: None: mapped types always drop modifiers

questions.q: What happens to note?: string in { [K in Extract<keyof Row, string>]: Row[K] }?
questions.explain: The keys no longer come straight from keyof Row, so the modifier is not copied. The looked-up type Row["note"] still includes undefined, so the property is required but may hold undefined.
options: It becomes a required note: string | undefined

questions.q: What is Partial<[string, number]>?
questions.explain: Homomorphic mapped types keep arrays and tuples as arrays and tuples, mapping each element. For a tuple, ? makes each element optional.

questions.q: What does { -readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] } do?
questions.explain: - removes a modifier and + (or no sign) adds it. The keys themselves stay; only the modifier changes. There is no built-in Mutable for this.

questions.q: With interface Options { pageSize?: number }, what is { [K in keyof Options]-?: Options[K] }?
questions.explain: -? removes the optional mark and the undefined it added to the property type. That is exactly Required.

questions.q: Is { +readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] } different from { readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] }?
questions.explain: The plus sign is optional and exists for symmetry with -. Both forms are shallow and compile-time only.
options: Yes: +readonly makes nested properties readonly too
No: + is the default, and both add readonly
Yes: +readonly only applies to optional properties
Yes: +readonly freezes the object at runtime

questions.q: What are the keys of { [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<K & string>}`]: () => T[K] } for T = { balance: number; currency: string }?
questions.explain: The as clause computes a new name for each key. Capitalize uppercases the first letter of each literal, and the template literal adds the prefix.

questions.q: Why does the renaming use K & string instead of just K?
questions.explain: Capitalize<S extends string> needs a string. K & string is K for string keys and never for symbols, so symbol keys disappear from the result.
options: Because keyof T may include number and symbol keys, and Capitalize only accepts strings; the intersection keeps the string keys
Because template literals require an intersection

questions.q: In { [K in keyof T as T[K] extends Function ? never : K]: T[K] }, what happens to a method?
questions.explain: Mapping a key to never in the as clause filters it out. That is how you remove keys by value type or by name while keeping the mapped type homomorphic.
options: It becomes a property of type never
It is removed, because a key mapped to never produces no property
It is kept but made optional

questions.q: With type KeysOfType<T, V> = keyof { [K in keyof T as T[K] extends V ? K : never]: T[K] }, why is discountKobo?: number not in KeysOfType<Invoice, number>?
questions.explain: The check compares the full property type. Use KeysOfType<Invoice, number | undefined> if optional numbers should be included, and handle the undefined case in the code that uses them.
options: Because optional properties are never mapped
Because its type is number | undefined, which is not assignable to number
Because of a bug in TypeScript

questions.q: What is { [E in PaymentEvent as E["type"]]: E }, where PaymentEvent is a union discriminated by type?
questions.explain: After in you may loop over any union, as long as as turns each member into a key. This builds an event map from a discriminated union, the base of typed handlers.
options: A syntax error: only keys can follow in
An object type with one property per event type, whose value is that event's member of the union

questions.q: What does the pattern { [K in keyof S]: Something<S[K]> }[keyof S] give you?
questions.explain: Indexing an object type with a union of its keys gives the union of its value types. Building a mapped type first lets you compute a value per key, then collect them, as EnvVarName does for every variable name in a schema.
options: An object type with the same keys as S
The union of Something<S[K]> for every key: the mapped type's values, collected by indexing with all keys
Only the value for the first key

questions.q: Why does DeepReadonly return Date unchanged instead of mapping over it?
questions.explain: A homomorphic mapped type visits every key, including methods such as getUTCFullYear, but only public ones: a class with a #private field, once mapped, is no longer assignable to that class. Stop the recursion at class instances you use, such as Date and Map.
options: Because mapping a class instance produces a plain object type listing all its methods, which is unreadable in errors, and which drops private fields, so a mapped class stops matching the class itself
Because mapped types cannot see methods

questions.q: Why is the first branch of DeepReadonly<T> T extends (...args: any[]) => any ? T?
questions.explain: A mapped type only copies properties. A function's ability to be called is a signature, not a property, so the recursion must leave functions as they are.
options: Because mapping a function type over its keys would drop its call signature, leaving an object you cannot call
Because functions cannot be stored in objects

questions.q: What does type Prettify<T> = { [K in keyof T]: T[K] } & {} change?
questions.explain: An identity mapped type visits every key of an intersection and produces a single object type, so editors and Equal see { id: string; roomId?: string } instead of Omit<…> & Partial<…>.
options: Only how the type is displayed and compared: it flattens an intersection into one object type

questions.q: Why does validators[key](transfer[key]) fail to compile when key: keyof Transfer?
questions.explain: This is the correlated-union limit. Use a generic helper with K extends keyof T, or a local, commented assertion.
options: Because validators[key] is a union of functions, which needs an argument that suits all of them, and TypeScript does not track that both lookups use the same key
Because keyof cannot be used with mapped types

questions.q: In setting<T, const E extends string>(d: { env: E; parse: (raw: string) => T; default?: NoInfer<T> }), what does NoInfer prevent?
questions.explain: Without NoInfer, a parser returning number and a default of "3" would infer T as number | string and compile. With it, the default is only checked against T.
options: It prevents the default from being used at runtime
It stops T being inferred from the default, so T comes from the parser and a default of the wrong type is an error

questions.q: What does const E extends string do for a call like setting({ env: "PORT", … })?
questions.explain: A const type parameter asks for the narrowest inference, like as const would. The literal is what lets EnvVarName list "PORT" rather than string.
options: It infers E as the literal "PORT" instead of widening to string, without as const at the call site
It checks that the environment variable exists

questions.q: The config loader ends with config as ConfigOf<S>. Why is an assertion needed there?
questions.explain: Code that builds values from keys, strings or recursion lives outside what the type checker can follow. Keep such assertions in one small function and test it.
options: Because the loader is badly written
Because a runtime recursion over Object.entries cannot be proven by the compiler to build the recursive computed type, even though it does
Because ConfigOf is not a real type
Because frozen objects have no type

questions.q: Why does the loader treat PAYSTACK_TIMEOUT_MS="" (or only spaces) as missing?
questions.explain: A timeout of 0 would make every request fail at once. Treating blank values as missing means they get the default, or a clear "is required" error.
options: Because empty strings cannot be stored in objects
Because an empty variable usually means "not configured", and parsing it would give wrong values such as Number(""), which is 0
Because TypeScript does not allow empty strings
Because environment variables cannot be empty

questions.q: With type DeepPartial<T> = { [K in keyof T]?: DeepPartial<T[K]> }, what is DeepPartial<{ tags: string[] }>["tags"]?
questions.explain: The mapped type also maps into the array, element by element, and ? on array elements adds undefined. For overrides, arrays are usually replaced as a whole, so many DeepPartial versions stop at arrays.

questions.q: Why does the config parser check with a regular expression? What does this print?
questions.explain: Number("") is 0 and parseInt stops at the first bad character, so neither can be trusted with config values alone. The parser checks the whole string's shape before converting.

questions.q: Define Balances and Rates as mapped types over Currency, and write totalInNaira(balances: Balances, rates: Rates): number that converts every balance (in minor units) to naira. Loop over the CURRENCIES array.
questions.explain: ₦45,000 plus $120 at 1,500 plus £50 at 2,000 is ₦325,000. The mapped types require a balance and a rate for every currency, so adding one to CURRENCIES makes both objects fail to compile until they are updated.

questions.q: A product form holds a Draft<Product> (every field optional and writable). Finish finish(draft): return the list of missing fields from REQUIRED, or the finished product when nothing is missing.
questions.explain: The starter's as Product accepted an incomplete draft. The solution reports every missing field, then narrows each value with a check the compiler can see (it cannot connect "the missing list is empty" to the individual fields), and builds a real product.

questions.q: Implement getters so it returns a getX() function for each key of the source, matching the Getters<T> type.
questions.explain: The runtime name rule (uppercase the first letter, add get) must match the type's rule, `get${Capitalize<K>}`. The final assertion connects the two; a test like this one keeps them in sync.

questions.q: Build EventMap from the ShipmentEvent union with a mapped type, write a Handlers object with one handler per event type, and print the handler results for the events in order.
questions.explain: EventMap keys each member by its type, so each handler's event parameter is inferred as the right member: signedBy only exists in the delivered handler. The loop needs the usual correlated-union assertion.

questions.q: Write KeysOfType<T, V> with key filtering, and use it in numericSummary, which prints key=value for the chosen numeric fields.
questions.explain: Keys whose value type is not assignable to number are mapped to never and disappear, so "name" or "breakfast" cannot be passed. Inside the generic function, the value still needs as number.

questions.q: Finish envVarNames: walk a nested schema and collect every env name, in order. A node is a setting when it has a string env property.
questions.explain: The runtime walk mirrors the recursive type: settings contribute their name, groups contribute the names inside them. Object keys keep their insertion order, so the list follows the schema.

questions.q: Write deepFreeze<T>(value: T): DeepReadonly<T> that freezes every nested plain object and array, then show that the nested object is frozen.
questions.explain: Object.freeze is shallow, like Readonly. Recursing first and then freezing each level makes the runtime match the DeepReadonly type, which is what the final assertion claims.
